disease_info: Bipolar II Disorder is characterized by a recurrent course of major depressive episodes alternating with hypomanic episodes, without any history of full manic episodes. Hypomanic periods involve a noticeable change in mood and energy that is observable by others but typically less severe than mania and not markedly impairing by themselves, though they often precede or follow disabling depressive episodes. The condition often begins in late adolescence or early adulthood and can be precipitated or unmasked by psychosocial stressors, sleep disruption, or substance use. It is distinguished from unipolar depression by the presence of hypomania and from Bipolar I Disorder by the absence of past mania and generally less severe mood elevation, though overall morbidity from recurrent depression can be substantial.

narrative.personality: Gustavo is a gritty, laid-back yet competitive firefighter who channels his artistic curiosity into mentoring and creative projects, but tends to be disorganized with practical details like budgeting and scheduling.
narrative.stressor: Over the past year, Gustavo has been pushing hard to complete his fire-captain certification while still taking frequent frontline shifts, often volunteering for complex HazMat calls to prove himself. The combination of high-stakes incidents, erratic overnight schedules, and studying on his days off gradually eroded his usual relaxed balance, especially as he felt increasing pressure to be a role model for younger bilingual recruits and the main financial support for his household. After a particularly intense wildfire deployment followed by a stretch of back-to-back overtime, his mood and energy began to swing more noticeably, with coworkers and his spouse both commenting that he seemed like a different person from week to week. When his captain pulled him aside about recent conflicts at the station and his wife expressed concern about how "amped up" and then "drained" he seemed at home, he agreed to see a psychiatrist at the department’s urging.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My wife and guys at the station keep saying I’m way more wound up and snappy than usual, like I’m on overdrive and can’t let stuff go.”

narrative.personality: David is a meticulous yet adaptable logistics worker whose curiosity about street art fuels ambitious, community-minded projects and an almost compulsive tendency to over-plan and optimize.
narrative.stressor: David’s onset followed a cluster of changes: he moved out of his mother’s apartment into a shared place with friends, took on a more demanding shift at the warehouse, and started talking with management about a possible promotion to operations supervisor. Excited to prove himself, he began redesigning parts of the warehouse layout on his own time, volunteering for extra shifts, and simultaneously throwing himself into organizing a small community art-and-food drive with his neighborhood group. Over several weeks, friends and coworkers noticed that he seemed to bounce between being intensely driven and outgoing—with a constant stream of new plans—to periods where he withdrew and lost interest in the very projects he had initiated, but he brushed it off as just being busy. When his supervisor cautioned him about taking on too many initiatives at once and his roommate complained that his constantly "amped up" energy was disrupting the household and then abruptly flipping to him barely leaving his room, David became worried that something more than stress was going on and agreed to a mental health referral through the warehouse’s employee assistance program.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I feel like I’m running on high gear all the time, jumping into project after project and can’t seem to slow my body down.”

narrative.personality: Dwayne is a quiet, precision-focused engineer who enjoys solitary, methodical hobbies and tends to over-plan and worry, favoring predictability and detailed organization in nearly every aspect of life.
narrative.stressor: In his late fifties, Dwayne began experiencing age-related health concerns—mild hypertension, joint aches that limited his woodworking and car restoration, and the first serious discussion with his doctor about eventually cutting back work hours. These changes unsettled his long-standing sense of control and predictability; he responded by tightening his routines, tracking every metric of his health, and meticulously reworking retirement budgets and plans. Over time, his family noticed that his mood and energy seemed to shift in phases, with stretches where he became unusually driven and short-tempered about getting projects and health regimens "just right," followed by quieter, withdrawn periods where his usual enjoyment of hobbies and mentoring at the coding meetup faded. After a minor health scare that turned out to be benign but left him feeling uncharacteristically volatile and argumentative at home and at work, his wife suggested that what he was going through didn’t look like his usual worry, leading him to consult a psychiatrist at his primary care provider’s recommendation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My wife says I’ve been more on edge and keyed up than usual, getting irritated over every little thing, and I don’t recognize myself in how I react.”
